nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1990 Jan 1. T. Duane Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory
Note: Author and date assigned based on when SLHs were written at Mote.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Trinectes maculatus
Common Name:  Hogchoker

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthys
      Order: Plueronectiformes
      Family: Soleidae

Other Common Names:  northern round sole (835), American broad sole (255) , sole (312
834).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Said to be delicious eating, but it is so small that it is of no commercial value (51). The young are frequently sold in the aquarium trade (327). Harvested in the Manatee River for the aquarium trade (1021).
Recreational: No known recreational fishery.

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role: Important as forage for other fish species.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  From Maine (rarely) and Massachusetts and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to Panama and Venezuela (327 788 937).
Within Study Area: Common in Tampa Bay, but not reported outside the bay proper (938). Frequently found as young in Florida freshwater rivers.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: Catadromous; the young run up rivers as far as 240 km (312 314 327 834). Found inshore in the summer and in deeper water in the winter (312). Young usually found upriver in spring and summer, and the spawners move down river in the summer (940). Some older individuals overwinter upstream, but some remain downstream (940). In the Myakka River, young of the year are most numerous upriver in the spring, but are taken downstream in the fall, with the largest individuals occurring at the river mouth (942).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Found in coastal waters to 75 m (788), but usually restricted to shallow inshore waters (860). Common in bays and shallow Gulf waters to 25 fm (327). Also found in freshwaters up to hundreds of miles upstream (788 835).
Substrate: Reported from mud, sand, and silt bottoms (378 938).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body: Eggs: Collected in the Chesapeake Bay area in temperatures from 14.7 to 30.1 C (940).

nodes.title: Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Springer and Woodburn (664) collected young and adults in Tampa Bay at temperatures ranging from 19.9 to 29.1 C.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs: Dove1 (940) collected eggs between 0 and 24 % in Chesapeake Bay, but found them to be most abundant at salinities of 10 to 16 %.
Larvae: Larvae move into low salinity waters (940 941). In the Myakka River, Florida, late post-larvae and early juveniles are most abundant in freshwaters 22 km or more upriver (942) .
Juvenile/adults: Springer and Woodburn (664) collected specimens in Tampa Bay at salinities ranging from 6.6 to 32.0 %, but reported that larger individuals were taken in higher salinities. In Texas, they have been collected in salinities ranging from 3.7 to 33.7 % (255). Found in salinities from 0 % (443 939) to 50 % (651). Collected in fresh spring water in the Charlotte Harbor area (789), and in Silver Spring (943). Although they apparently prefer brackish waters (3781, sexually mature individuals are not usually present in freshwater (938).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode: Sexual reproduction with broadcast spawning.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Gravid females found only in marine localities in Florida, and spawning presumably occurs in the mouths of bays and estuaries (938). Sexually mature individuals are not usually found in freshwater (938). Spawning occurs in the spring and summer in Chesapeake Bay (312), and in the summer in the lower Patuxent River (940). Spawning is reported to begin when temperatures are about 200 C (940). A protracted spawning season has been reported in Florida, with peak activity in the late spring and summer (938). A May to November spawning period has been suggested in southwest Florida with peak larval densities occurring from June through October in the Myakka River (942).
Fecundity: Females mature at a size as small as 10.8 cm (312). An 87 mm SL female contained 11,075 eggs and a 108 mm female had 23,075 eggs (938). One female 165 mm long contained 54,000 eggs (312).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body: Eggs: Eggs hatch in 26 to 34 hours at 23 to 24 C (314).

nodes.title: Larvae
nodes.body: Juveniles/Adults: Size at one year of age reported to range from 51 to 76 mm (51). For individuals ranging from 50 to 148 mm, the following growth increments during each year of life were reported: I=40 mm, II=26, III=16, IV=16, v=13, VI=12, and VII=8 (944). Maximum size of adults is given as 20 cm (312 788). All females are mature at the age of four, and a size of 111-114 mm (51 940 944). Can live to an age of 7 (944). Average length at each age was given by Mansueti and Pauly (944) as I=41.7 mm, II=65.6, III=83.8, IV=100.1, V=113.5, VI=124.4, and VII=131.0.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Feed primarily on worms and small crustaceans (312 327).
